page: Google Cloud Platform n2-highmem-8 is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance configured with 8 vCPUs and 64 GB of RAM, yielding an 8:1 RAM-to-vCPU ratio. It is powered by an Intel Xeon processor operating at a base frequency of 2.8 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The CPU allocation is dedicated, featuring 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled (2 threads per core). The processor includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 33 MB of L3 cache. This instance does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPUs, and it provides zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark evaluations place the instance's multi-core CPU performance and memory bandwidth in the average tier. The stress-ng multi-core test scored 7393.32, while the Geekbench multi-core score reached 4476.0. Memory read-only bandwidth for cached small blocks is measured at 413.33 GB/sec, and uncached large block read and write speeds are 52.02 GB/sec and 40.05 GB/sec, respectively. However, single-core capabilities are relatively weak, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1405.78. Specialized workloads like ray tracing and image processing also perform in the bottom 25%.

Given its high memory density of 8 GB per vCPU, the n2-highmem-8 is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound applications that do not require intensive parallel GPU computing or high-speed local NVMe storage. It is well-suited for database operations, caching layers like Redis (achieving 7.13 million SET operations per second in testing), and static web serving with 7.05 GB/sec throughput. Conversely, it is poorly suited for large language model inference, where prompt processing for a 7B model drops to a poor 10.36 tokens/sec.
description: The Google Cloud Platform n2-highmem-8 is an x86_64 virtual machine featuring 8 dedicated vCPUs and 64 GB of RAM, powered by an Intel Xeon processor running at 2.8 GHz. With 4 physical cores and hyper-threading, it delivers a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8 GB per core. The instance lacks bundled local storage and GPU accelerators. Performance benchmarks indicate average multi-core CPU capabilities and solid memory bandwidth, with uncached large block read speeds at 52.02 GB/sec and Redis SET operations reaching 7.13 million per second. However, single-core processing and complex tasks like ray tracing or LLM inference are weak. This configuration is qualitatively cost-effective for memory-intensive workloads such as database management, caching, and web serving, rather than compute-heavy or AI-driven applications.
